etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Latin aestimātus, past participle of aestimō, older form aestumō (“to value, rate, esteem”); from Old Latin *ais-temos (“one who cuts copper”), meaning one in the Roman Republic who mints money. Compare Middle English estymatt (“reputed”). See also the doublet esteem, as well as aim.

definitions.definition: A rough calculation or assessment of the value, size, or cost of something.
(construction and business) A document (or verbal notification) specifying how much a job is likely to cost.

quote.citation: 1928, Lawrence R. Bourne, chapter 3, in Well Tackled!‎[1]:
quote.text: “They know our boats will stand up to their work,” said Willison, “and that counts for a good deal. A low estimate from us doesn't mean scamped work, but just that we want to keep the yard busy over a slack time.”

definitions.definition: An upper limitation on some positive quantity.

quote.citation: 1992, Louis de Branges, “The convergence of Euler functions”, in Journal of Functional Analysis, →DOI, page 185:
quote.text: The desired norm estimate is now obtained from the identity... [referring to an earlier statement saying that a certain norm is less than or equal to a certain expression]

definitions.definition: To calculate roughly, often from imperfect data.

quote.citation: 1965, Ian Hacking, Logic of Statistical Inference‎[2]:
quote.text: I estimate that I need 400 board feet of lumber to complete a job, and then order 350 because I do not want a surplus, or perhaps order 450 because I do not want to make any subsequent orders.

quote.citation: 2003, Alexander J. Field, Gregory Clark, William A. Sundstrom, Research in Economic History‎[3]:
quote.text: Higher real prices for durables are estimated to have reduced their consumption per capita by 1.09% in 1930,  […]

definitions.definition: To judge and form an opinion of the value of, from imperfect data.

quote.citation: 1691, [John Locke], Some Considerations of the Consequences of the Lowering of Interest, and Raising the Value of Money. […], London:  […]  Awnsham and John Churchill, […], published 1692, →OCLC:
quote.text: It is by the weight of silver, and not the name of the piece, that men estimate commodities and exchange them.

quote.citation: 1870, John Campbell Shairp, Culture and Religion in Some of Their Relations:
quote.text: It is always very difficult to estimate the age in which you are living.
